title: Cross-Gram overlap and principal angles
subtitle: G2 lecture 042000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: Measuring overlap between subspaces
slides.lead: Principal angles measure the best possible directional alignment between two subspaces.
body: Choose isometric frames E and F whose columns form orthonormal bases of subspaces U and V. The cross-Gram matrix C=E*F records all pairwise inner products between the chosen frame vectors.
The entries change when we change bases, but the singular values do not. That invariance makes the singular values natural candidates for intrinsic overlap measurements.
slides.takeaway: Cross-Gram singular values measure overlap independently of the chosen orthonormal frames.

slides.title: One-dimensional overlap
slides.lead: For unit vectors u and v, their acute line angle is determined by the magnitude of their inner product.
body: The orthogonal projection of v onto span(u) has length |⟨u,v⟩|. If the lines meet at acute angle θ, that length is cos θ.
Changing the sign or phase of a chosen basis vector cannot change the angle between the underlying lines. The absolute value removes this irrelevant coordinate choice.
slides.takeaway: Cosine is the length of the projected unit direction.

slides.title: Why the singular values are intrinsic
slides.lead: Changing orthonormal frames changes C by unitary factors on the left and right.
body: If E is replaced by EA and F by FB for unitary A and B, the new overlap matrix is A*C B. Left and right multiplication by unitaries preserves all singular values.
Therefore the singular values of E*F depend only on U and V. Their arccosines, ordered between 0 and π/2, are the principal angles.
slides.takeaway: Principal angles survive every orthonormal change of coordinates.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 042000 · Why the singular values are intrinsic

slides.title: A pair of planes in three dimensions
slides.lead: Let U=span(e₁,e₂), and tilt only its e₂ direction toward e₃.
body: Set V=span(e₁, cos φ e₂+sin φ e₃), where 0<φ<π/2. With those displayed orthonormal frames the cross-Gram matrix is diag(1, cos φ).
The first principal angle is zero because the planes share e₁. The second is φ: the e₂ direction must tilt out of U by φ to reach V.
slides.takeaway: Shared directions give zero angles; tilted directions give positive angles.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 042000 · A pair of planes in three dimensions

slides.title: Paired principal vectors
slides.lead: An SVD of the cross-Gram matrix constructs optimal pairs of aligned directions.
body: Choose orthonormal vectors u_i in U and v_i in V so that ⟨u_i,v_j⟩=0 when i≠j and |⟨u_i,v_i⟩|=cos θ_i. A convenient phase choice makes each paired overlap nonnegative.
For each pair, the component of v_i along u_i has length cos θ_i; its perpendicular component has length sin θ_i. This is the geometric seed of the cosine–sine decomposition.
slides.takeaway: SVD turns many overlapping directions into independent principal pairs.

slides.title: Projector formula for overlap
slides.lead: The overlap Gram operator is itself a compression of the target projection.
body: Write Q=FF* for the orthogonal projection onto V. Then CC*=E*FF*E=E*QE. This is a positive contraction: every unit x in U has projection length at most one.
Its eigenvalues are the squared cosines of the principal angles, so the cross-Gram singular values lie in [0,1].
slides.takeaway: The cosine-squared operator is the projection Q viewed in U coordinates.

slides.title: Complementary escape gives the sine
slides.lead: Any framed vector splits into its Q component and its perpendicular remainder.
body: Because E*E=I and Q is a projection, E*(I−Q)E=I−CC*. The eigenvalues of this positive operator are 1−cos²θ_i=sin²θ_i.
Hence the same principal vectors diagonalize overlap and escape. This orthogonal complement identity is the bridge from principal angles to sine-theta perturbation bounds.
slides.takeaway: Cosine and sine are two complementary views of the same frame.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 042000 · Complementary escape gives the sine

slides.title: Unequal dimensions require a convention
slides.lead: A rectangular cross-Gram matrix has only min(dim U, dim V) paired principal angles.
body: If U is a plane and V a line contained in U, the one paired angle is zero. But a direction in U perpendicular to V also exists and has escape angle π/2.
Both descriptions are legitimate: the shorter principal-angle list records paired overlap; the U-directed list also records unpaired directions. State which convention a theorem uses.
slides.takeaway: The number of angles depends on whether unmatched dimensions are included.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 042000 · Unequal dimensions require a convention

slides.title: The two directional overlap maps
slides.lead: The overlap map and its adjoint contain the same paired cosine values.
body: The matrix C=E*F maps target-frame coordinates to source-frame coordinates; its adjoint C*=F*E reverses that direction. Their nonzero singular values agree, by the singular-value decomposition.

What differs between the two directions is the number of unmatched zero singular values when the frame dimensions are unequal. This explains why a directed angular description may need more information than the list of paired principal angles.
slides.takeaway: Paired cosine values are symmetric, but unpaired directions are directional.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 042000 · The two directional overlap maps

slides.title: A full calculation to retain
slides.lead: Rebuild the tilted-plane example without referring to a drawing.
body: Construct E=[e₁,e₂] and F=[e₁,cosφ e₂+sinφ e₃]. Compute C=E*F, its singular values, and the two angles.
Then compute E*(I−Q)E directly and confirm that its diagonal entries are 0 and sin²φ. This checks both cosine and sine from one transparent example.
slides.takeaway: Cross-Gram SVD and complementary projection agree on the principal angles.
